nameStory: Cheyletiella blakei was named after researcher who first described this tiny mite species. The genus name Cheyletiella comes from Greek words meaning 'little claw,' referring to the distinctive claw-like structures these mites use to grip onto their hosts. Blake's walking dandruff mite is sometimes called this because the mites are so small they look like moving flakes of dandruff on a pet's fur.
description: Blake's walking dandruff mite is a microscopic parasite that lives on domestic cats, though it can temporarily bite humans too. These incredibly tiny mites are so small you'll never see individual ones with the naked eye - they're much smaller than a pinhead. What you might notice instead are the effects: cats scratching more than usual, or small itchy bumps on people who handle infected cats. This is a relatively uncommon parasite, but cases may be increasing in some areas.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Impossibly tiny - individual mites are microscopic and invisible to the naked eye, smaller than the period at the end of this sentence

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Creates the appearance of 'walking dandruff' - what looks like moving white flakes or specks in cat fur that seem to crawl slowly

idTips.label: Host Signs
idTips.description: Cats may scratch excessively, have flaky skin, or develop a scruffy coat texture that feels rougher than normal

idTips.label: Human Symptoms
idTips.description: People handling infected cats may develop small, intensely itchy red bumps that feel like mosquito bites but appear in clusters

habitat: Blake's walking dandruff mite lives exclusively on domestic cats, particularly indoor cats in homes, apartments, and shelters throughout New England. You won't find these mites free-living in nature - they require a cat host to survive. They're most commonly found in multi-cat households or places where cats are kept in close quarters.

seasonality.spring: Mite populations may increase as cats spend more time grooming and in closer contact during springtime activity. Indoor cats can be affected year-round.
seasonality.summer: Warm weather doesn't significantly affect these indoor parasites, though cats spending time outdoors may pick up infestations from other cats.
seasonality.fall: Mite activity continues unchanged as these parasites live in the controlled environment of heated homes rather than responding to outdoor temperature changes.
seasonality.winter: Indoor heating creates ideal conditions for mite reproduction, potentially making winter a peak time for infestations in house cats.

funFact: These mites are so light that they can actually become airborne and float through the air on tiny dust particles, which is how they sometimes spread between cats that never directly touch each other!
confusionNotes: The 'walking dandruff' appearance is often mistaken for regular dandruff, flea dirt, or dry skin. The key difference is that true dandruff doesn't move on its own - if those white flakes seem to crawl slowly across your cat's fur, you're likely seeing mites.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Blake's walking dandruff mite,' this species affects cats rather than dogs (other Cheyletiella species prefer dogs or rabbits). The term 'zoonosis' means it's a disease that can jump from animals to humans, though it can't complete its life cycle on people.
compareHints: Blake's walking dandruff mite is currently the only Cheyletiella species documented in New England, though other species in this genus affect dogs and rabbits. Compared to other tiny mites that might affect cats, Cheyletiella creates the distinctive 'walking dandruff' appearance rather than causing obvious bite marks or burrowing into skin like some other parasitic mites.
